Sonia / Caleb,

Thanks for the draft MSA — attached is Redwood's initial redline (Redwood_MSA_redline.pdf). We want to surface two narrow but important points that will determine whether we can proceed on your timeline:

1) Governing law: we prefer Washington State law (home state for key infrastructure and precedent we rely on). If GreenPath has a firm preference for another state, please say which and why.

2) Dispute resolution: Redwood prefers arbitration for monetary claims but needs an explicit carveout allowing either party to seek immediate injunctive or emergency relief in court to protect IP, customer data, or to stop data exfiltration. Practically: monetary/non-injunctive claims -> arbitration; injunctive/emergency relief -> short-term court proceedings (King County Superior Court or U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington).

We included a proposed short emergency-relief paragraph in the attachment (emergency-relief-draft.txt) that: (a) confirms carveout for injunctive relief, (b) includes streamlined notice/service and (c) requires parties to proceed to arbitration for any follow-on monetary relief.

If you can accept the Washington-law + injunctive carveout approach, we can finalize quickly. Otherwise please send your counter-redline and we can hop on a 30-minute call to resolve.

Requested next step: please respond by 2028-07-15 (3 business days) if possible — our procurement needs to lock terms for the pilot.

Thanks,

Dylan Brooks

Dylan — thanks for the clear note and the redline. We discussed with our legal team and have a couple of points: 

1) Governing law: GreenPath strongly prefers New York law for commercial predictability across our vendor contracts. We can be flexible on venue for injunctive relief, but changing governing law to Washington is a material ask for our legal team.

2) Dispute resolution: Our preference is a single forum for disputes (arbitration) to avoid parallel proceedings. That said, we are open to a limited carveout for emergency relief but would prefer the carveout to require that any emergency court action be brought in New York courts — we can agree to Washington for injunctive relief only if Redwood can accept New York law governing interpretation.

3) Class/collective relief: GreenPath's outside counsel wants a class-waiver and explicit confirmation that arbitration is the exclusive remedy for non-injunctive disputes.

I've attached GreenPath_MSA_counter_redline.pdf showing the edits (high level: New York law; arbitration seat: London ICC; emergency relief carveout with consent to comity).

We want to avoid a long back-and-forth. Two options from our side:
  - Option A: Keep New York governing law and allow injunctive relief in Washington courts (limited to emergencies) — need clause that New York law still applies to interpretation.
  - Option B: Washington law and Washington courts for injunctive relief, but in that case GreenPath asks that monetary claims be heard in arbitration seated in New York (ICC or AAA).

Can you advise which option Redwood prefers? If neither is acceptable, let's set a call tomorrow 10am PT.

—Caleb

Subject: Re: Redlines: governing law & dispute-resolution — Washington carveouts

Caleb — thanks for the clear options. Quoting your key asks below for clarity:

> Option A: New York governing law + injunctive relief allowed in Washington courts (emergency-only).
> Option B: Washington governing law + monetary arbitration seated in New York.

Our take: Redwood is comfortable with a split approach that preserves operational predictability and rapid emergency relief. Proposed compromise we can live with: 

- Governing law: Washington State law (substantive law).
- Arbitration: Exclusive forum for all claims seeking monetary relief or declaratory relief, administered by AAA/ICDR or agreed AAA rules; seat for arbitration: New York (neutral procedural forum).
- Emergency/injunctive relief carveout: Either party may seek temporary injunctive or emergency equitable relief in a court of competent jurisdiction without first invoking arbitration. For clarity: jurisdiction and venue for injunctive/emergency relief -> King County Superior Court or U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. Any emergency relief obtained shall be without prejudice to the parties' obligation to resolve remaining claims in arbitration.
- Class actions: Redwood prefers class/collective waiver language where permitted; we can include statutory carveouts.

Why this works: Washington law governs interpretation and substantive rights (helps our engineering and infra teams), while New York provides a neutral arbitration seat for efficient procedural administration. Injunctive relief must be enforceable quickly in our home forums because most of the critical systems and data are in WA.

I dropped a short, focused draft of the emergency clause in the shared Drive (see link) and attached it to our original redline. If that wording is acceptable to GreenPath's counsel, we can incorporate and sign. If you need us to shift to New York law (Option A), we would need compensating concessions (e.g., a stronger limitation on injunctive forum shopping and faster arbitration timelines).

Can we confirm by end of day 7/14 PT? If yes, I'll have legal (Marissa) give a final pass and we'll route for signature.

Best,
Dylan

Quick internal note — drafted a compact emergency-relief sentence we should push if GreenPath agrees to the split approach above. Paste below (feel free to use as-is):

"Notwithstanding the arbitration provision, either party may seek interim or emergency injunctive relief in a court of competent jurisdiction to prevent irreparable harm, including with respect to Confidential Information, Intellectual Property, or data security incidents; such relief shall be sought in King County Superior Court or the United States District Court for the Western District of Washington, without waiving any right to arbitration for monetary or declaratory relief."

Also recommend adding: (i) expedited notice to the other party (24 hours where practicable), (ii) agreement to lift any temporary orders after final arbitration award if arbitrator so orders, and (iii) service-of-process consent limited to emergency relief matters.

If you want, I can fold this into the redline and push to the Drive link.
